2027-07-25.title: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha
2027-07-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The law given through Moses: honour your father and mother
A people who did not turn to the one who struck them
Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord
Do not make void the word of God through your tradition
2027-07-25.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “The law is through Moses”; “Punishment to Israel for false doings”; “Be proud in the Lord Jesus”; “Do not reject the word of God to keep your tradition”. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 5:16–6:3; Isaiah 9:8–21; 2 Corinthians 10:1–18; Mark 7:1–23. St James the Apostle (25 July) gives way to the Sunday. Today is also the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly (instituted by Pope Francis in 2021, kept near the feast of Sts Joachim and Anne). In the Latin calendar today is the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (the feeding of the five thousand, John 6).
2027-07-25.verse: You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.
theo: The Fourth Sunday of Kaitha puts side by side two things that people often think are rivals: the commandment of God and the traditions of men. The Gospel opens with a scene any Kerala household would know. The Pharisees and some scribes who had come from Jerusalem notice that the disciples eat without first washing their hands. Washing before meals, and washing cups, pots and bronze kettles, was a devout custom of pious Jews, and in itself a good one; Jesus himself does not condemn the custom. What he condemns is the use of such a custom to set aside what God has plainly said. Their question, “Why do your disciples not live according to the tradition of the elders?”, is answered with a sentence from Isaiah, who prophesied that this people “honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me.” We should hear this as a debate among the people of God, in which Jesus speaks as a Jewish teacher to other Jewish teachers, and as a warning to every community that has traditions, including ours.

Then Jesus gives a precise example, and it is about parents. “Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother.’” That is the fourth commandment of the first reading: “Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land.” Some, however, had arranged that whatever support a son might have given his parents could be declared “Corban,” dedicated to God, and so withheld from the father and mother who needed it. It looked pious, and it killed a commandment. The lesson is plain: no offering, no donation, no ornament on the church and no vow can replace the daily care of an old father or mother. “Then you no longer permit doing anything for a father or mother, thus making void the word of God through your tradition.” On this Sunday, when many parishes and families remember grandparents and the elderly, the Gospel asks a very practical question: who is sitting alone in the back room of our house?

The first reading takes us to Horeb, where Moses recalls the ten words and the fire. “These words the Lord spoke with a loud voice to your whole assembly at the mountain, out of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, and he added no more. He wrote them on two stone tablets.” The people were afraid, and said: “Today we have seen that God may speak to someone and the person may still live.” God's law is not a burden placed on us to catch us out. It is the voice of the living God out of the fire, spoken so that people may live. The commandment about parents stands at the head of the second table because the family is where every child first learns to hear a voice that asks for love and gives life in return.

Isaiah shows what happens when a people hears no voice at all. “The people did not turn to him who struck them, or seek the Lord of hosts.” The leaders led them astray, and the prophets who taught lies were the tail; the orphans and widows found no compassion; wickedness burned like a fire; “Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh.” Brother devours brother, and the fire of the sin of a people finally burns the people. It is a hard reading, and it is not a prophecy about other people only. Wherever a family fights over land and inheritance, wherever relatives stop speaking for years, we are in the world of Manasseh and Ephraim. The Lord's hand, says the prophet, “is stretched out still”: stretched out in judgment, and, as the Church reads it, still stretched out to call us back.

Paul's short passage in the second reading supplies the remedy: measure yourself by the Lord and not by one another. The Corinthians' rivals commended themselves and compared themselves with each other, which, says Paul, “does not show good sense.” He will boast only within the field that God has assigned to him, and he will not boast in the labours of others. The whole passage closes with a sentence from Jeremiah that he also uses in his first letter: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For the Church in Kerala the sentence is a good guard against the pride of old families, rich parishes, big feasts and fine buildings. “For it is not those who commend themselves that are approved, but those whom the Lord commends.” The Lord commends the one who honours a father and a mother, who keeps a clean heart, and who listens when God speaks from the fire.
conn: “Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12); “Honor your father and mother” is “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2).

“My child, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him as long as he lives” (Sirach 3:12); “Listen to your father who begot you, and do not despise your mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23:22).

“The Lord said: Because these people draw near with their mouths and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their worship of me is a human commandment learned by rote” (Isaiah 29:13).

“It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but it is what comes out of the mouth that defiles” (Matthew 15:11); “For it is from within, from the human heart, that evil intentions come” (Mark 7:21).
“Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29); at Pentecost “divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them” (Acts 2:3).

“Let those who boast boast in this, that they understand and know me, that I am the Lord; I act with steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth” (Jeremiah 9:24); “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).
altar: The word Qurbana comes from the same root as Corban, the gift that is brought near to God. At the Holy Qurbana nothing is withheld from God and nothing is taken from the poor: what we bring is bread and wine, and with it our work, our care for our parents and our children. Christ the true Offering gives himself to us, and the heart, not only the lips, is nourished.

The altar and the family table are not rivals. The Lord who gives his Body and Blood at the altar sends us home to wash the feet and share the meal of the father and mother, the grandfather and grandmother, who are waiting there. Whoever goes from the Qurbana and forgets the old person at home has taken the Corban and left the commandment.
outline: Washed hands and clean hearts: what do the traditions of our homes and parishes serve?
Point 1 · The voice out of the fire
The Ten Words are God's own voice, given for life; the fourth commandment opens the table of love.
No offering replaces the care of parents; the word of God must not be made void by our tradition.
Point 3 · The fire that devours and the one who boasts
Manasseh and Ephraim: families that devour each other; boast only in the Lord.
“You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.” Let us return to the commandment.
live: Visit, telephone or sit with a parent, a grandparent or an elderly neighbour this week, and ask them to tell you a story of their faith.
Ask whether any gift you give to the Church or a charity is a way of avoiding a duty at home. Meet the duty at home first.
Before going to the Holy Qurbana this week, say a short prayer: “Create in me a clean heart.” Then name one bitter word you will not speak.
If two relatives are not speaking, try to bring them together this week, or at least pray for them by name.
fathers: Honour of parents is the first lesson of love. Do not think that you have done enough when you have given gifts at the altar and left your father to want. The one who is cruel to the parent who bore him cannot be pleasing to the Lord whom he has not seen.

What makes a person unclean is not the food that goes in but the heart that is evil. Wash the heart, and you will have washed all. The Lord looks first at the inside of the cup, and the inside is the heart.
Those who boast in the Lord boast in what is true, since they know that whatever good they have is a gift. The one who boasts in himself builds on sand; the one who boasts in the Lord builds on rock.
magis: The fourth commandment opens the second table of the Decalogue. It shows us the order of charity: after God, we are to honour our parents, who have given us life and handed on to us the knowledge of God.
Respect for parents shows itself in obedience while children live in the home, and in later years in gratitude, care and company when parents are old, ill, lonely or in distress.

The Tradition that comes from the apostles hands on what they received from Jesus' teaching and example. It is to be distinguished from the theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions born over time in the local Churches, which the Church's authority may keep, modify or abandon.
The Ten Commandments belong to God's Revelation. At the same time they teach us the true humanity of man, and they are given as a covenant in which God and the people are bound together.
saints: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha. St James the Apostle (25 July) gives way to the Sunday. World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. In the Latin calendar, the Seventeenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.

Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne. Wed 28: St Alphonsa. Thu 29: St Martha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. Karkidakam, the heart of the monsoon, begins in mid-July: many families read the Bible and pray the rosary together at home in the long wet evenings.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-25.prayer: Lord God, you spoke to your people out of the fire and gave them your commandments that they might live. Teach us to honour our fathers and mothers, to care for them in their old age and to respect the elders of our parish and of every family. Keep our worship from becoming a habit of the lips while the heart is far from you. Heal every family in which brother is set against brother, and make us boast in you alone. Through the prayers of Sts Joachim and Anne, grandparents of your Son, bless the old people of our homes. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: the Ten Words spoken out of the fire; honour your father and mother, that it may go well with you.
Isaiah: the people did not turn to him who struck them; the fire of wickedness; Manasseh devoured Ephraim.
Paul: do not compare yourselves with others; boast only in the Lord.
Mark: the tradition of the elders must not void the commandment of God; the example of Corban and the care of parents.
2027-07-25.action: Spend time with an elderly person in your family this week, and do one concrete thing for them.
2027-07-25.question: Is there any gift or custom of mine that lets me escape what God plainly asks of me?
kidsaint: Saint Monica lived in North Africa about sixteen hundred years ago. She loved her son Augustine very much, and when he went far from God she prayed and cried for him for many years. God heard her. Augustine became a great saint and a bishop, and he wrote that he owed much to his mother's tears. Lesson: love and honour your parents and grandparents, and pray for them every day.
2027-07-25.special: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha. World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly.
term: A Hebrew word for a gift dedicated to God (Mark 7:11). It comes from a root meaning to draw near, which is also the root of the Syriac word Qurbana, the offering we call the Holy Qurbana. A gift is truly Corban only when it does not take away what God commands us to give to others.

family.explain: Jesus said that some people honoured God with words, but their hearts were far away. God's fourth commandment says: honour your father and your mother. Some people said, ‘I have given my money to God, so I cannot help my parents.’ Jesus said that was wrong. To love God is also to look after the old people in our home. Grandfathers and grandmothers are God's special gifts to us.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents and for every old person who is lonely.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can do for an old person this week: a visit, a call, a drawing, a prayer?”

illus: In a parish in the hills of Idukki (a story told to illustrate the reading) a family gave a large sum for the new bell tower, and their name was cut into the stone. The vicar, who visited homes on Saturdays, found the grandmother of that family in a back room, with a single plate and no one to talk to; the son was busy with the building committee. He said nothing at first. At the dedication he blessed the tower, and then asked the family to bring grandmother to the front row. ‘The bell calls us to God,’ he said quietly, ‘but I think this lady is the first bell of your house.’ The son wept. From that day the old woman sat at the family table every evening. The vicar often said afterwards that he had only repeated Jesus' words about Corban.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you showed us that the word of God must never be made void by our traditions. Gather us now, and teach us to honour our fathers and mothers and to keep our hearts clean. Amen.
share: Honor your father and your mother (Deuteronomy 5:16). How do I honour my parents or grandparents, living or dead?
This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me (Mark 7:6). Where is my prayer only on the lips?
The people did not turn to him who struck them (Isaiah 9:13). What do I need to turn back to the Lord about?
Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (2 Corinthians 10:17). Of what am I proud, and is it a gift?
pm.resp: Lord, let your word never be made void in us.
interc: For the Church, that her traditions may always serve the commandments of God and the Gospel.
For grandparents and the elderly, that they may be honoured, cared for and never left alone.
For families divided by quarrels over land, money or old hurts, that they may find peace.
For those who give to the Church and the poor, that their giving may come from a loving heart.
For parents and children of our parish, that they may honour one another in love.
pm.close: Father of every family, you gave us your Son to be born among a family and to be honoured by a mother. Bless the elderly among us and make us a household that keeps your commandment. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today the Gospel brings us to the dinner table. Some Pharisees and scribes notice that the disciples of Jesus eat without washing their hands first. For them it was a matter of tradition, and a good tradition. But Jesus uses the occasion to teach something deeper.

He quotes Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me” (Mark 7:6). It is possible to say all the prayers, to keep all the customs, and still have a heart that is far from God. And then Jesus says, “You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition” (Mark 7:8).

He gives an example. God said: “Honor your father and your mother.” But some people said, ‘What I would have given to my parents is Corban, it is dedicated to God,’ and so they gave nothing to their old parents. They looked pious, but they made void the word of God (Mark 7:10–13).

Brothers and sisters, this is very close to our life. A donation to the church is a good thing. A big feast is a good thing. But if our old father or mother sits alone in the back room, if no one has time to talk to them, then something is wrong. Today is the day we remember grandparents and the elderly. The first reading reminds us: “Honor your father and your mother… so that it may go well with you” (Deuteronomy 5:16).

Isaiah shows us what happens when people forget God and each other: “Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh” (Isaiah 9:21). Brother turns against brother. Let us ask where in our families there are such quarrels, and let us be the first to make peace.

And Saint Paul tells us how to live: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17). Not in our family name, our money or our good works, but in the Lord. This week, let us honour our parents, keep our hearts clean, and boast only in him. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: honour your father and your mother. That means your grandparents too! Some grown-ups said they were too busy because they were giving to God, and Jesus said that was wrong. This week, give your grandparents a hug, tell them a story, or draw them a picture. That is a way of loving God, too!

intro: Theme: “You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”
On the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha: the voice of God from the fire, Corban and the care of parents, and boasting only in the Lord.

points.h: The voice of God out of the fire
sub: The Ten Words are spoken for life.
The fourth commandment opens the table of love.
Today we have seen that God may speak and a person may live.
q: Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the Lord your God is giving you.
for indeed our God is a consuming fire.
points.apply: Honour a parent or elder this week with one concrete act: a visit, a call, a meal together.

sub: Heart far from God, lips near.
A gift cannot replace the care of a father or mother.
Tradition must serve the word of God.

points.h: The fire that devours, and the one who boasts
sub: Compare yourself with the Lord, not with others.
q: Manasseh devoured Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh, and together they were against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away; his hand is stretched out still.

points.apply: Make one move this week toward peace with a relative with whom you are not speaking.

concl: God's commandments are his own voice, spoken for life, and they begin with honouring those who gave us life.
Let no tradition, gift or pride make the word of God void in us: let us boast only in the Lord.
2027-07-25.resolve: This week, honour a parent or an elder in a concrete way, seek peace in the family, and keep the heart clean before the Lord.
